note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/10 Group 2/10.1 Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals, magnesium to barium, and.md
outline: Group 2 metals form $M^{2+}$ ions. Down the group, reactions with water and dilute acids generally become more vigorous. Oxides and hydroxides are basic; carbonates release carbon dioxide with acids. Nitrates decompose to oxides, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen; carbonates decompose to oxides and carbon dioxide. Thermal stability increases down the group. Hydroxides become more soluble but sulfates less soluble down the group.

misconceptions.statement: Magnesium reacts vigorously with cold water.
misconceptions.refutation: Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water; calcium, strontium and barium react more readily.

misconceptions.statement: A Group 2 oxide effervesces when added to water.
misconceptions.refutation: Oxide plus water makes a hydroxide; no gas forms. A soluble oxide may disappear into a colourless solution.
misconceptions.contrast: Barium oxide in water shows no bubbles.

misconceptions.statement: A carbonate reacts with acid to make carbonic acid only.
misconceptions.refutation: Carbonate plus acid gives a salt, carbon dioxide and water.
misconceptions.contrast: Magnesium carbonate with hydrochloric acid releases carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.statement: Heating a Group 2 nitrate gives the metal or nitrogen monoxide.
misconceptions.refutation: It gives the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.
misconceptions.contrast: Balance oxygen after fixing the oxide and nitrogen dioxide coefficients.

misconceptions.refutation: Larger metal cations polarise the anion less, so decomposition needs more heat down the group.
misconceptions.contrast: Barium carbonate is more stable than magnesium carbonate.

misconceptions.statement: Hydroxides and sulfates follow the same solubility trend.
misconceptions.refutation: Hydroxide solubility increases while sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2.
misconceptions.contrast: Barium hydroxide is soluble but barium sulfate is insoluble.

Q is a mixture of a Group 2 oxide and a Group 2 sulfate. Q contains equal amounts of the two
compounds.

9701-10.1.1.motivate: Why do calcium and barium fizz in water while magnesium scarcely does? The same two outer electrons drive their reactions, but become easier to remove down the group.
9701-10.1.1.establish: Group 2 metals form $M^{2+}$ ions. With oxygen they form oxides, for example $2Mg(s)+O_2(g)\rightarrow2MgO(s)$. With cold water they form hydroxides and hydrogen, for example $Ca(s)+2H_2O(l)\rightarrow Ca(OH)_2(aq)+H_2(g)$. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but with steam forms $MgO$ and $H_2$. With dilute hydrochloric acid they form chlorides and hydrogen: $Mg(s)+2HCl(aq)\rightarrow MgCl_2(aq)+H_2(g)$. With dilute sulfuric acid they form sulfates and hydrogen: $Mg(s)+H_2SO_4(aq)\rightarrow MgSO_4(aq)+H_2(g)$. An insoluble sulfate coating may slow the reaction. Water reactions become more vigorous from magnesium to barium.
9701-10.1.1.connect: The trend follows greater shielding and atomic radius down Group 2: losing the two outer electrons becomes easier.
9701-10.1.1.note:
- Oxygen gives a white metal oxide.
- Water gives hydroxide and hydrogen.
- Dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid gives salt and hydrogen.
- Cold-water reactivity rises from Mg to Ba.
9701-10.1.1.self_explain: Why does calcium release hydrogen from cold water faster than magnesium, and what balanced equation describes calcium's reaction?

9701-10.1.2.motivate: A white oxide can vanish in water without fizzing; a white carbonate fizzes in acid. Identifying the starting compound tells you which products to expect.
9701-10.1.2.establish: Group 2 oxides are basic and react with water to give hydroxides: $BaO(s)+H_2O(l)\rightarrow Ba(OH)_2(aq)$. Hydroxides dissolve to different extents, making alkaline solutions; carbonates do not appreciably react with water alone. Oxides and hydroxides neutralise dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to make the chloride or sulfate and water, for example $MgO(s)+H_2SO_4(aq)\rightarrow MgSO_4(aq)+H_2O(l)$ and $Ca(OH)_2(aq)+2HCl(aq)\rightarrow CaCl_2(aq)+2H_2O(l)$. Carbonates with either dilute acid make salt, carbon dioxide and water: $MgCO_3(s)+2HCl(aq)\rightarrow MgCl_2(aq)+CO_2(g)+H_2O(l)$ and $CaCO_3(s)+H_2SO_4(aq)\rightarrow CaSO_4(s)+CO_2(g)+H_2O(l)$. Insoluble sulfate may coat a carbonate and slow its reaction.
9701-10.1.2.connect: These are acid-base reactions. The carbonate produces water as well as carbon dioxide, so its products differ from a metal plus acid.
9701-10.1.2.note:
- Oxide plus water gives hydroxide, without gas.
- Oxide or hydroxide plus acid gives salt and water.
- Carbonate plus acid gives salt, carbon dioxide and water.
- Carbonates show no appreciable reaction with water alone.
9701-10.1.2.self_explain: Why does barium oxide dissolve without bubbles in water, while magnesium carbonate bubbles in hydrochloric acid?

9701-10.1.3.motivate: Heating a Group 2 carbonate or nitrate reveals a dependable product pattern; the temperature needed also tells you how stable the compound is.
9701-10.1.3.establish: On heating, a Group 2 carbonate gives the oxide and carbon dioxide: $CaCO_3(s)\rightarrow CaO(s)+CO_2(g)$. A Group 2 nitrate gives the oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: $2Ca(NO_3)_2(s)\rightarrow2CaO(s)+4NO_2(g)+O_2(g)$. The nitrate equation needs two formula units to avoid a fractional oxygen coefficient. Thermal stability of both carbonates and nitrates increases from magnesium to barium. The larger cations lower down the group have lower charge density and polarise the large anions less, so more heat is required to decompose them.
9701-10.1.3.connect: This same change in cation size helps explain why the metals react more readily even though their salts become harder to decompose.
9701-10.1.3.note:
- Carbonate heat: oxide plus carbon dioxide.
- Nitrate heat: oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen.
- Both thermal stabilities increase down Group 2.
9701-10.1.3.self_explain: Write the balanced equation for heating magnesium nitrate and predict whether barium nitrate needs more or less heat.

9701-10.1.4.motivate: A trend lets you predict the behaviour of an unfamiliar Group 2 element from its position, but each property needs the correct direction.
9701-10.1.4.establish: From magnesium to barium, atomic radius and shielding increase and the outer electrons are lost more easily. Thus metal reactions with oxygen, cold water and dilute acids tend to become more vigorous, though an insoluble sulfate layer can affect an acid observation. Their oxides form basic hydroxides with water; oxides and hydroxides neutralise acids, and carbonates release carbon dioxide with acids. Both nitrates and carbonates become more thermally stable down the group, so higher decomposition temperatures are required. Hydroxides become more soluble, whereas sulfates become less soluble. Use these directions to predict observations, precipitates and comparative reaction temperatures. Metal melting points are irregular, so use supplied data instead of claiming a smooth trend.
9701-10.1.4.connect: Prediction combines the reaction patterns with the separate solubility and thermal-stability trends.
9701-10.1.4.note:
- Metal reactivity increases down the group.
- Carbonate and nitrate thermal stability increases.
- Hydroxide solubility increases; sulfate solubility decreases.
- Metal melting points are irregular.
9701-10.1.4.self_explain: Predict how strontium compares with calcium in its cold-water reaction, carbonate decomposition and hydroxide solubility.

9701-10.1.5.motivate: Two barium compounds behave very differently in water: its hydroxide can give a strongly alkaline solution, while its sulfate forms a white precipitate.
9701-10.1.5.establish: State the two opposite solubility trends separately. The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group from magnesium hydroxide to barium hydroxide. The solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group from magnesium sulfate to barium sulfate. Magnesium hydroxide is only slightly soluble; barium hydroxide is considerably more soluble. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, while barium sulfate is very sparingly soluble. Thus a saturated barium hydroxide solution can have a higher pH than a saturated magnesium hydroxide solution, and mixing barium ions with sulfate ions gives a white barium sulfate precipitate.
9701-10.1.5.connect: Use solubility to decide whether a product remains dissolved or appears as a precipitate in the reactions of oxides, hydroxides and acids.
9701-10.1.5.note:
- Hydroxide solubility increases from Mg to Ba.
- Sulfate solubility decreases from Mg to Ba.
- Barium sulfate is a white, very insoluble solid.
9701-10.1.5.self_explain: Which is more soluble, barium hydroxide or magnesium hydroxide? Which sulfate is more likely to precipitate?
